messages.subject: Different AIC for null model between PRESENCE and unmarked
messages.subject_clean: Different AIC for null model between PRESENCE and unmarked
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I need some help for analyses that i compared between PRESENCE and unmarked.
I create sames models on PRESENCE and unmarked, i got sames AIC for all model except for the null model. The difference is quite important. Does anyone have any idea where the difference might come from? If you need an overview of a part of my script, my data or anythhing else, tell me.

                                                      nPars      AIC        delta      AICwt    cumltvWt
psi(.)p(vent + Temp + Temp²)     5         376.14    0.00       0.6370     0.64
psi(.)p(vent)                                    3        377.82    1.69       0.2742     0.91
psi(.)p(Temp)                                 3        382.37     6.23       0.0283     0.94
psi(.)p(soleil)                                  3        382.49     6.35       0.0267     0.97
psi(.)p(nuage)                                 3        382.51    6.37       0.0264     0.99
psi(.)p(.)                                           2       385.03     8.90       0.0075     1.0

Thanks for your help
Goulvenn.

messages.subject_clean: Different AIC for null model between PRESENCE and unmarked
messages.body_plain:
Can you show the coefficient estimates for the null model from unmarked and from PRESENCE?

Do you have missing values in any of your covariates? If so unmarked might be dropping sites where detection covariates in a given model are missing, meaning the datasets for the null model and the rest of the model would not be the same. I'm not sure if/how PRESENCE handles that.

Ken

> https://groups.google.com/g/unmarked/c/tn3vqvNOPvI/m/RVMLDqPTCgAJ
>
> You can do something similar with ubms output but it is a bit more complicated because you have the posterior distribution of projected occupancy at each site and primary period, rather than point estimates. Here's a quick example with code and output using the frogs dataset provided with unmarked.
>
> -----------------------------
>
>     set.seed(123)
>     suppressMessages(library(ubms))
>     data(frogs)
>     umf <- formatMult(masspcru)
>     umf@y[umf@y>1] <- 1
>     obsCovs(umf) <- scale(obsCovs(umf))
>     # Make a fake treatment site covariate
>     siteCovs(umf) <- data.frame(treat=sample(c("A","B"), numSites(umf), replace=TRUE))
>
>     ## Use 1/4 of data just for run speed in example
>     umf <- umf[which((1:numSites(umf)) %% 4 == 0),]
>
>     # Fit in ubms
>     # Unsurprisingly treatment coefficient CI overlaps 0 since we made it up
>     (mod_stan <- stan_colext(~treat, ~1, ~1, ~JulianDate, umf, chains=3, iter=300, refresh=0))
>
>     ##
>     ## Call:
>     ## stan_colext(psiformula = ~treat, gammaformula = ~1, epsilonformula = ~1,
>     ##     pformula = ~JulianDate, data = umf, chains = 3, iter = 300,
>     ##     refresh = 0)
>     ##
>     ## Occupancy (logit-scale):
>     ##             Estimate    SD   2.5% 97.5% n_eff  Rhat
>     ## (Intercept)   1.4028 0.422  0.638  2.31   358 0.994
>     ## treatB       -0.0321 0.598 -1.322  1.25   359 0.998
>     ##
>     ## Colonization (logit-scale):
>     ##  Estimate    SD  2.5%  97.5% n_eff Rhat
>     ##     -1.23 0.466 -2.19 -0.389   370    1
>     ##
>     ## Extinction (logit-scale):
>     ##  Estimate    SD  2.5% 97.5% n_eff  Rhat
>     ##     -2.91 0.429 -3.85 -2.15   390 0.999
>     ##
>     ## Detection (logit-scale):
>     ##             Estimate    SD   2.5%   97.5% n_eff Rhat
>     ## (Intercept)   -0.133 0.111 -0.339  0.0858   432    1
>     ## JulianDate    -2.108 0.154 -2.407 -1.8230   391    1
>     ##
>     ## LOOIC: 716.484
>     ## Runtime: 5.508 sec
>
>     # Get projected occupancy at each site and primary period
>
>     # Dimensions: nsamples x (# sites x # primary periods in site-major order)
>     # see ?ubms::projected
>     proj_occ <- projected(mod_stan)
>
>     # Re-arrange into array samples x primary period x nsite
>     proj_occ <- array(proj_occ, c(nsamples(mod_stan), umf@numPrimary, numSites(umf)))
>
>     # Calculate mean occupancy across sites in each sample and primary period
>     # This ignores treatment for now
>     proj_mean <- apply(proj_occ, c(1,2), mean)
>
>     # Summarize across samples to get mean occupancy per primary period
>     colMeans(proj_mean)
>
>     ## [1] 0.7913132 0.7964553 0.7993061 0.8008328 0.8015986 0.8019320 0.8020245
>
>     # Now get estimates by treatment using the proj_occ array
>
>     # Instead of calculating overall mean, calculate mean for each treatment
>     mean_by_treat <- function(x){
>       treat <- siteCovs(umf)$treat
>       c(treatA = mean(x[treat == "A"]),
>         treatB = mean(x[treat == "B"]))
>     }
>
>     # Apply over each sample and primary period
>     proj_treat <- apply(proj_occ, c(1,2), mean_by_treat)
>
>     # Calculate mean estimate across all samples
>     treatment_est <- apply(proj_treat, c(1,3), mean)
>
>     # 95% CI
>     lower <- apply(proj_treat, c(1,3), quantile, 0.025)
>     upper <- apply(proj_treat, c(1,3), quantile, 0.975)
>
>     # Build plot
>     plot(1:7-0.1, treatment_est[1,], ylim=c(0.5, 1), type='o', col='blue',
>         ylab="Occupancy and 95% CI", xlab="Primary period")
>     segments(1:7-0.1, lower[1,], 1:7-0.1, upper[1,], col='blue')
>     lines(1:7+0.1, treatment_est[2,], type='o', col='red')
>     segments(1:7+0.1, lower[2,], 1:7+0.1, upper[2,], col='red')
>     legend('bottomright', lty=1, col=c("blue","red"), legend=c("A","B"),
>             title="Treatment")
>
>
>
> On Friday, May 20, 2022 at 12:44:38 AM UTC-4 vishnur...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I'm trying to run a multi-season occupancy model (two seasons: prefire and postfire) across two different treatments (baited and unbaited). I'm using ubms so as to include a random effect 'region' on my multiseason model.
> >
> > umf <- unmarkedMultFrame(y= fox_det[,-1], yearlySiteCovs = list( baiting=baiting),
> >                          siteCovs = list(treatment=treatment, region=region),
> >                          obsCovs = list(time.det= time, site = site), numPrimary = 2)
> > model <- stan_colext(~treatment+(1|region), ~1,~1,~1, umf, chains=3,iter=300)
> >
> > How do I estimate occupancy values for both seasons across my two treatments? I tried using
> > nd <- data.frame(treatment= c("unbaited","baited"),
> >                  time.det= c("prefire","postfire"))
> > predict(model,submodel="state",newdata=nd,re.form=NA)
> >
> > But that only gives me occupancy values for the second season across the two treatments. I'm essentially trying to get occupancy values for the combination of seasons and treatment (4 values in total). I'm still a beginner at this, so any help would be highly appreciated. Thanks a lot!
> >
> >

Interesting and intimidating thread for those of us whose knowledge of MLE algorithms and the behind the scenes working of these programs isn't as strong.

If someone weren't comparing unmarked and PRESENCE, but just running models in unmarked, they would have missed this issue, right? messages.body_plain:
Starting values are unlikely to be an issue in most cases, but it's always a good idea to try a few sets of starting values anytime you use maximum likelihood, regardless of the software program being used.

Sensitivity to starting values is most likely to occur when the model has lots of parameters, or when the data suggest that occupancy or detection probability is close to 0 or 1. These boundary cases aren't defined on the logit scale. You will usually notice a problem when this occurs. For example, in Goulvenn's case, the estimate of occupancy was essentially 1, and the SE was NaN. That should prompt you to try other starting values.

--
Richard Chandler
Associate Professor
Wildlife Ecology and Conservation
Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources
University of Georgia
762-499-4085
http://chandlerlab.uga.edu/

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

The same problem reported for occupancy models in this thread is also happening in N-mixture models. Although estimates for a given model are similar between these packages, AIC values are very different. We have seen the same problem with different datasets. Anyone experiencing the same issues?

Saludos!

Eduardo A. Silva-Rodriguez, Med.Vet., PhD
Instituto de Conservación Biodiversidad y Territorio <http://www.forestal.uach.cl/instituto/conservacion-biodiversidad-territorio/>
Facultad de Ciencias Forestales y Recursos Naturales
Universidad Austral de Chile
https://publons.com/researcher/2844442/eduardo-a-silva-rodriguez/ <http://www.researcherid.com/rid/B-1854-2010>

El jue, 2 jun 2022 a las 9:56, Alex Wolf (<aw...@scenichudson.org>) escribió:

> Very helpful and practical advice - thank you, Dr. Chandler!
>
> On Thu, Jun 2, 2022 at 9:51 AM Richard Chandler <rcha...@warnell.uga.edu> wrote:
> > Starting values are unlikely to be an issue in most cases, but it's always a good idea to try a few sets of starting values anytime you use maximum likelihood, regardless of the software program being used.
> >
> > Sensitivity to starting values is most likely to occur when the model has lots of parameters, or when the data suggest that occupancy or detection probability is close to 0 or 1. These boundary cases aren't defined on the logit scale. You will usually notice a problem when this occurs. For example, in Goulvenn's case, the estimate of occupancy was essentially 1, and the SE was NaN. That should prompt you to try other starting values.

I feel like I would have just gone with the unmarked results using starting values of 0, assuming decent goodness of fit.  Until default start values are addressed, is there a best practice for unmarked to test for this?  E.g., should one always rerun models with informed starting values after running models with starting values of 0?  Do we know how common this issue is?

messages.subject_clean: AW: [unmarked] Occu() issue. Hessian is singular/starting values
messages.body_plain:
Dear Isabelle,

here are a couple of quick ideas:
It is often a good idea to build up a more complex model in steps of increasing complexity. That is, perhaps even start with the simplest model, with two intercepts for (in your case) psi and p, and then add one covariate at a time. And then use the solutions of the previous model in your progression as the inits for the current model
In unmarked you must supply one initial value for each parameter in the model and in the same order in which they appear when you do “coef(fm)” (where fm is a fitted model object). You provide inits as a list, e.g., as follows: “inits <- c(-0.3333, 0.453)”. Then, when you fit the model, you add an argument “starts = inits” in the call to function occu.
When you do this step-up approach of model building, you add in an NA for the new parameter that does not appear in the previous model in your progression. So, if the previous model is the Null model with the two intercepts for psi and p and your current model has one continuous covariate in the detection part of the model, then you would do something like “inits <- c(coef(fm)[1], NA, coef(fm)[2])”.

Best regards --- Marc

Betreff: [unmarked] Occu() issue. Hessian is singular/starting values

Hello,

I'm trying to use occu() to estimate the detection probability of trapping invasive crabs in 3 trap types over 5 areas. My data includes the calculated effort (catch per unit effort of total crabs caught/per trap soak night). The dataset contains over 4500 individual trap checks, and 35,000 invasive crabs removed, from 1 month of surveying. There are a lot of NAs.

The code is coming along nicely, but I got stuck trying to add my co variates. My best guess is that I need to add starting values, but I have no idea how to find them. The error message is requesting 9 starting values, I assumed those have to do with the 3 trapping methods, 5 areas, and effort. So I attempted to use my table to provide starting values. Is it asking for psi coefficients? I’m not sure how to go about finding those.

I’ve copied the code over and all warnings and errors, sorry if it’s a bit long. Most of these warnings are totally okay. Any advice on how to find starting values would be greatly appreciated! I’m new to unmarked.

> egcdp <- isabelle_lisy[,c("P.1","P.2","P.3","P.4","P.5","P.6","P.7","P.8","P.9",

+                           "P.10","P.11","P.12","P.13","P.14","P.15","P.16","P.17",

+                           "P.18","P.19","P.20")]

> egcdp.umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y = egcdp,

+                                siteCovs = data.frame(Method = isabelle_lisy$Method,

+                                                      Area = isabelle_lisy$Area),

+                                obsCovs = list(effort = isabelle_lisy[,c("eff1",

+                               "eff2","eff3","eff4","eff5","eff6","eff7","eff8",

+                               "eff9","eff10","eff11","eff12","eff13","eff14",

+                               "eff15","eff16","eff17","eff18","eff19","eff20"),]))

> #this second model adds all co variates

> EGC2 <- occu(~Method +Area +effort ~1,egcdp.umf)

Warning messages:

1: 2 sites have been discarded because of missing data.

2: In truncateToBinary(designMats$y) :

  Some observations were > 1.  These were truncated to 1.

3: Hessian is singular. Try providing starting values or using fewer covariates.

Error in occu(~Method + Area + effort ~ 1, egcdp.umf, starts = c()) :

  The number of starting values should be 9

In addition: Warning messages:

2: In truncateToBinary(designMats$y) :

  Some observations were > 1.  These were truncated to 1.

#9 starting values? one for each of the 3 methods, 5 areas, and effort?

#grabbed the first value for each in the table

> EGC2 <- occu(~Method +Area +effort ~1,egcdp.umf, starts= c(12, 7, 122, 12, 19, 40, 226, 63, 12))

Warning messages:

1: 2 sites have been discarded because of missing data.

2: In truncateToBinary(designMats$y) :

  Some observations were > 1.  These were truncated to 1.

> EGC2 <- occu(~Method +Area +effort ~1,egcdp.umf, starts= c("Fukui","Minnow",

+                 "Shrimp","FloatingDock","Marsh","MuddyHatchery","NorthernExtent",

messages.body_plain:
As Marc suggests, starting off with simpler models helps figuring out starting values.  But one of the simpler models with your data suggests that more complicated models with occu can't be supported with your data. (If someone on this list disagrees, they will certainly let you and me know.)

The model with a single parameter for occupancy and three parameters for detection using "Method" (Fukui, Minnow, and Shrimp) results in occupancy essentially being estimated to be 1.0 and all three of the methods having estimated detection probabilities very close to 1.  That doesn't leave much to explain by any other predictor.  Here's the output as to why I say that:

>   results <- occu(~Method ~1, egcdp.umf)
> # Call:
> # occu(formula = ~Method ~ 1, data = ufo)
> #
> # Occupancy:
> #  Estimate  SE      z P(>|z|)
> #      15.4 598 0.0257    0.98
> #
> # Detection:
> #            Estimate    SE         z P(>|z|)
> # (Intercept)     11.81    65  0.181732   0.856
> # MethodMinnow    -8.64    65 -0.132830   0.894
> # MethodShrimp    12.65 15006  0.000843   0.999
> #
> # AIC: 16.39769
>
> # psi
> 1-1/(1+exp(results@opt$par[1]))
> # 0.9999998
>
> # p(Fukui)
> 1-1/(1+exp(results@opt$par[2]))
> # 0.9999926
>
> # p(Minnow)
> 1-1/(1+exp(results@opt$par[2]+results@opt$par[3]))
> # 0.9600037
>
> # p(Shrimp)
> 1-1/(1+exp(results@opt$par[2]+results@opt$par[4]))
> # 1

The occu output matches exactly one of the outputs that you presented.

So I wonder if occu (i.e., predicting presence or absence) as opposed to predicting counts might be more informative.

Jim

messages.subject: Optimal detection history length for camera trap studies
messages.subject_clean: Optimal detection history length for camera trap studies
messages.body_plain:
Hello!
My name is Ellery Lassiter and I am a graduate student in the USGS Coop Unit at University of Arkansas. Our lab recently finished a group project using camera trap data from Snapshot USA to investigate abundance and occupancy patterns of opossums across their range in the U.S.

When determining what interval to use for the 'detection histories' for our occupancy analysis, I noted a fair degree of variation in the literature concerning detection history length, even within a single species.

Therefore, I was curious if there is an optimal detection history length for camera trap studies when analyzing the data using an occupancy framework? Or is this impossible to standardize due to how one defines site, sampling occasion, and season (and the interplay among these)?

Thanks for any additional information and insight into this matter!

Regards,
Ellery

--
Ellery Lassiter
Graduate Student | BISC
University of Arkansas
evla...@uark.edu

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ellery,

Others likely have better insights here, but I think the key considerations are that if the sampling occasions are too short (e.g., 1 minute or something) there may be some lack of independence (and having very many sampling occasions will slow things down). I guess very long (i.e., fewer) sampling occasions will lead to wider CI, larger RMSE for the point estimate, things like that. If the "true" p-star is very close to 1, there may not be much practical difference in how things are split or lumped.

Seems difficult to posit any general rules--might depend on how many things there are, how they move around, how they move around with respect to one another, probably other things too. Could try to quantify an adequate interval building off of something like doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13308 <https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13308>. If using finer intervals and concerned about lack of independence, could employ a test like doi.org/10.1002/ece3.2292 <https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.2292>, or use a model like doi.org/10.1890/09-0321.1 <https://doi.org/10.1890/09-0321.1>, or estimate some effect of detection in the previous occasion (or some longer memory effect), and so forth.

John

messages.subject: Colext, uneven time periods
messages.subject_clean: Colext, uneven time periods
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Just started a new position and I'm analyzing a bit of an odd dataset in terms of the seasons. Amphibian surveys were done in 2010, 2011, 2012, 2015, 2018 and 2021 at 62 sites (usually 3 visits per year). Not sure if it was budget or time but surveys started out yearly but going forward are done every 3 years.

This is my first foray into dynamic models and my initial thought was that we'd have to throw out the 2010-2011 data and stick with a three year interval (2012, 2015, 2018, 2021). Our main goal is to look at occupancy trends over time.

One note, I'm actually doing this in stan_colext but don't think that matters in this context.

Thanks,
Griffin

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] False positive occupancy
messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] False positive occupancy
messages.body_plain:
Dear Prashant,

I have to look this stuff up myself .... here is some text from the AHM2 book on the issue of these data types (p. 405).

"Data can be of three types and are
specified using the “type” argument in unmarkedFrameOccuFP. Occasions are defined to belong to
one of the three data types and all or multiple data types can be combined into the same model.
For Type 1 data, the detection process is assumed to meet the assumptions of the standard occupancy
model where only false-negative errors occur, and false-positive detections are assumed to be absent. If all
your data are of this type only, you should use the occu function. The detection parameter p, which is
modeled using the detformula, is the only observation model parameter for these data.
For Type 2 data, both false-negative and false-positive detection errors are allowed. If all data are
of this type, the likelihood follows Royle and Link (2006). Both p (the true-positive detection
probability, called p11 in our notation here) and the false-positive detection probability, p10 in our
notation, described by fpformula, are estimated. In unmarked, the parameter p10 is labeled fp.
For Type 3 data, observations include both certain detections (known to be true positives) and
uncertain detections (that may be false positives). For the former we use the terms “certified,”
“verified,” or “confirmed” detections synonymously to indicate that a detection is known to be a true
positive. The observation model for Type 3 data contains the parameters p11 and p10 but, in addition,
contains the new parameter b which is the probability that a true positive detection is verified to be
certain. Miller et al. (2011) termed the model for Type 3 data to be a “multiple detection state”
modeldbecause detections are represented by two distinct states, certain and uncertain, leading to a
multi-state model. In contrast, when both Type 1 and Type 2 data occur together, the estimator is
equivalent to the "multiple detection method" model described in Miller et al. (2011), which is just a
traditional two-state occupancy model, but where p10 is assumed to be 0 for part of the data. Of course,
all three types of data can be accommodated together in the same model, and this would be a “multiple
detection-state, multiple method” model. On the other hand, each of the types could be thought of as
simply a different method, producing independent data sets which are included together as distinct
likelihood contributions to the overall likelihood in what might be considered an “integrated model”
(Chapter 10). Modeling Type 3 data is discussed in Section 7.4 below."

And then later (p. 411), we have this bit which is insightful:

"We declare the two different data types via the type argument. The data are organized such that
occasions 1-3 represent the Type 1 data from method 1, and occasions 4-7 are the Type 2 data from
method 2.

type <- c(nsurveys1, nsurveys2, 0)

When creating the unmarkedFrameOccuFP data object note that Method must be defined as an
observational covariate. Note also that we could model variation in p10 using site or observation
covariates.

summary(umf1 <- unmarkedFrameOccuFP(y = y, obsCovs = list(Method = Method),
type = type)) # not shown"

So, type is a vector that gives the number of occasions that are in type 1, type 2 and type 3, respectively.

Best regards --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Dear Marc,

Thank you so much for the help. I am now able to run my models and define my type of data which is type 3 data in the form type(0, 0, 5) since my all occasions have type 3 form. I got the results as expected however when I added my survey-specific covariates age and gender, where age is continuous and gender is categorical I got this error:
Error in model.frame.default(FPformula, obsCovs, na.action = NULL) :
invalid type (list) for variable 'gender'

I had listed my survey-specific covariates as list(age, gender)however while running models it was showing the above error. Please suggest how will I include my survey-specific covariates in my models to include the effect of categorical covariates on False-positive detection probability.

Thank You
Prashant

On Monday, June 20, 2022 at 1:37:09 AM UTC+5:30 Kery Marc wrote:
> Dear Prashant,
>
> I have to look this stuff up myself .... here is some text from the AHM2 book on the issue of these data types (p. 405).
>
> "Data can be of three types and are
> specified using the “type” argument in unmarkedFrameOccuFP. Occasions are defined to belong to
> one of the three data types and all or multiple data types can be combined into the same model.
> For Type 1 data, the detection process is assumed to meet the assumptions of the standard occupancy
> model where only false-negative errors occur, and false-positive detections are assumed to be absent. If all
> your data are of this type only, you should use the occu function. The detection parameter p, which is
> modeled using the detformula, is the only observation model parameter for these data.
> For Type 2 data, both false-negative and false-positive detection errors are allowed. If all data are
> of this type, the likelihood follows Royle and Link (2006). Both p (the true-positive detection
> probability, called p11 in our notation here) and the false-positive detection probability, p10 in our
> notation, described by fpformula, are estimated. In unmarked, the parameter p10 is labeled fp.
> For Type 3 data, observations include both certain detections (known to be true positives) and
> uncertain detections (that may be false positives). For the former we use the terms “certified,”
> “verified,” or “confirmed” detections synonymously to indicate that a detection is known to be a true
> positive. The observation model for Type 3 data contains the parameters p11 and p10 but, in addition,
> contains the new parameter b which is the probability that a true positive detection is verified to be
> certain. Miller et al. (2011) termed the model for Type 3 data to be a “multiple detection state”
> modeldbecause detections are represented by two distinct states, certain and uncertain, leading to a
> multi-state model. In contrast, when both Type 1 and Type 2 data occur together, the estimator is
> equivalent to the "multiple detection method" model described in Miller et al. (2011), which is just a
> traditional two-state occupancy model, but where p10 is assumed to be 0 for part of the data. Of course,
> all three types of data can be accommodated together in the same model, and this would be a “multiple
> detection-state, multiple method” model. On the other hand, each of the types could be thought of as
> simply a different method, producing independent data sets which are included together as distinct
> likelihood contributions to the overall likelihood in what might be considered an “integrated model”
> (Chapter 10). Modeling Type 3 data is discussed in Section 7.4 below."
>
> And then later (p. 411), we have this bit which is insightful:
>
> "We declare the two different data types via the type argument. The data are organized such that
> occasions 1-3 represent the Type 1 data from method 1, and occasions 4-7 are the Type 2 data from
> method 2.
>
> type <- c(nsurveys1, nsurveys2, 0)
>
> When creating the unmarkedFrameOccuFP data object note that Method must be defined as an
> observational covariate. Note also that we could model variation in p10 using site or observation
> covariates.
>
> summary(umf1 <- unmarkedFrameOccuFP(y = y, obsCovs = list(Method = Method),
> type = type)) # not shown"
>
> So, type is a vector that gives the number of occasions that are in type 1, type 2 and type 3, respectively.
>
> Best regards --- Marc
>
>
>

> > "Data can be of three types and are
> > specified using the “type” argument in unmarkedFrameOccuFP. Occasions are defined to belong to
> > one of the three data types and all or multiple data types can be combined into the same model.
> > For Type 1 data, the detection process is assumed to meet the assumptions of the standard occupancy
> > model where only false-negative errors occur, and false-positive detections are assumed to be absent. If all
> > your data are of this type only, you should use the occu function. The detection parameter p, which is
> > modeled using the detformula, is the only observation model parameter for these data.
> > For Type 2 data, both false-negative and false-positive detection errors are allowed. If all data are
> > of this type, the likelihood follows Royle and Link (2006). Both p (the true-positive detection
> > probability, called p11 in our notation here) and the false-positive detection probability, p10 in our
> > notation, described by fpformula, are estimated. In unmarked, the parameter p10 is labeled fp.
> > For Type 3 data, observations include both certain detections (known to be true positives) and
> > uncertain detections (that may be false positives). For the former we use the terms “certified,”
> > “verified,” or “confirmed” detections synonymously to indicate that a detection is known to be a true
> > positive. The observation model for Type 3 data contains the parameters p11 and p10 but, in addition,
> > contains the new parameter b which is the probability that a true positive detection is verified to be
> > certain. Miller et al. (2011) termed the model for Type 3 data to be a “multiple detection state”
> > modeldbecause detections are represented by two distinct states, certain and uncertain, leading to a
> > multi-state model. In contrast, when both Type 1 and Type 2 data occur together, the estimator is
> > equivalent to the "multiple detection method" model described in Miller et al. (2011), which is just a
> > traditional two-state occupancy model, but where p10 is assumed to be 0 for part of the data. Of course,
> > all three types of data can be accommodated together in the same model, and this would be a “multiple

> > > model where only false-negative errors occur, and false-positive detections are assumed to be absent. If all

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am playing around with some multi-season occupancy models in Unmarked, but I have this issue. If I used two years (seasons or primary period), when I try to add “year-1” in the colonization and extinction part of the model it does not work, and I received this message.

 m2 <- colext(~1, ~year-1, ~1, ~1, umf)

Error in `contrasts<-`(`*tmp*`, value = contr.funs[1 + isOF[nn]]) :  contrasts can be applied only to factors with 2 or more levels

I tried exactly the same code but added two fake years more to test the script. So, I used a detection history across four years and all models ran well, including the derived parameters for the projected psi per year.

Is it correct to think that these models only apply to situations where we have more than two years or what can I do to include the year in the col and extinction parameters? (please see below how I added year as a covariate in case it´s wrong)

If I used a model with a covariate only in the initial occ such as m12 <-colext(~Dist.Ele,~1,~1,~1,umf), I can get the col/ext estimates for the first year (and the two years for p) and also the derived estimated occupancy probability for smoothed and projected for each year with their SE (which is actually our primary interest for now). I am just confused about why we can not add the year directly in the col(gamma) and ext(epsilon) part when we have two years (probably more a conceptual question).

Any insight would be highly appreciated.

thanks

All the best

L

--------

A bit of extra context

I created the year cov like this, hope is fine

n <- nrow(sp_DH1)   # number of sites, sp_DH_1 is the detection history df

T <- 2    # number of primary periods, years or seasons

J <- 21    # number of secondary periods (visits per season)

y <- as.matrix(sp_DH1)

# create a matrix indicating the year each site was surveyed.

year <- matrix(c('1','2'),  nrow(y), T, byrow=TRUE)

umf <- unmarkedMultFrame( y = y,

               numPrimary = 2, siteCovs = site_covs_s[,11:12], yearlySiteCovs = list(year = year))
*just in case, if I used any other continuos variable in gamma or epsilon it works (e.g. a site covariate that changes between seasons using a list)

--

School of Natural Resource Management

messages.body_plain:
If you have 2 years of data, you are only estimating 1 year of colonization and extinction probabilities (col and ext going from year 1 --> year 2). Thus you would only have a single value in the year factor covariate (year 1), and you can't get a coefficient estimate for a factor covariate with a single level.

unmarked allows you to supply values for all primary periods in the yearlySiteCovs in case you want to use them as part of the detection model, but the final primary period of covariates is automatically dropped from col/ext submodels since it won't be used.

Ken

> > > model where only false-negative errors occur, and false-positive detections are assumed to be absent. If all
> > > your data are of this type only, you should use the occu function. The detection parameter p, which is
> > > modeled using the detformula, is the only observation model parameter for these data.
> > > For Type 2 data, both false-negative and false-positive detection errors are allowed. If all data are
> > > of this type, the likelihood follows Royle and Link (2006). Both p (the true-positive detection
> > > probability, called p11 in our notation here) and the false-positive detection probability, p10 in our
> > > notation, described by fpformula, are estimated. In unmarked, the parameter p10 is labeled fp.

> > > contains the new parameter b which is the probability that a true positive detection is verified to be

messages.body_plain:
Dear Prashant,

thanks, this is interesting. Now, the gender effect are wonky in both analyses. They may correspond to so-called boundary estimates, i.e., when the estimate of a proportion falls exactly on 0 and 1. Then, the maximum likelihood estimates are not to be trusted. Such problems can be “weakly” diagnosed by parameter estimates that are large in absolute terms (e.g., about > 5 or so) and more still by SE estimates that are large (e.g., 10 or higher).

So, you ought to check whether the gender effect is estimable or whether perhaps all males have only nondetections and all females only detections.

Best regards  -- Marc

> > > >
> > > > "Data can be of three types and are
> > > >

> > > >
> > > > For Type 1 data, the detection process is assumed to meet the assumptions of the standard occupancy
> > > >
> > > > model where only false-negative errors occur, and false-positive detections are assumed to be absent. If all
> > > >
> > > > your data are of this type only, you should use the occu function. The detection parameter p, which is
> > > >
> > > > modeled using the detformula, is the only observation model parameter for these data.
> > > >
> > > > For Type 2 data, both false-negative and false-positive detection errors are allowed. If all data are
> > > >
> > > > of this type, the likelihood follows Royle and Link (2006). Both p (the true-positive detection
> > > >
> > > > probability, called p11 in our notation here) and the false-positive detection probability, p10 in our
> > > >
> > > > notation, described by fpformula, are estimated. In unmarked, the parameter p10 is labeled fp.
> > > >
> > > > For Type 3 data, observations include both certain detections (known to be true positives) and
> > > >
> > > > uncertain detections (that may be false positives). For the former we use the terms “certified,”
> > > >
> > > > “verified,” or “confirmed” detections synonymously to indicate that a detection is known to be a true
> > > >
> > > > positive. The observation model for Type 3 data contains the parameters p11 and p10 but, in addition,
> > > >
> > > > contains the new parameter b which is the probability that a true positive detection is verified to be
> > > >
> > > > certain. Miller et al. (2011) termed the model for Type 3 data to be a “multiple detection state”
> > > >
> > > > modeldbecause detections are represented by two distinct states, certain and uncertain, leading to a
> > > >
> > > > multi-state model. In contrast, when both Type 1 and Type 2 data occur together, the estimator is
> > > >
> > > > equivalent to the "multiple detection method" model described in Miller et al. (2011), which is just a
> > > >
> > > > traditional two-state occupancy model, but where p10 is assumed to be 0 for part of the data. Of course,
> > > >
> > > > all three types of data can be accommodated together in the same model, and this would be a “multiple
> > > >
> > > > detection-state, multiple method” model. On the other hand, each of the types could be thought of as
> > > >
> > > > simply a different method, producing independent data sets which are included together as distinct
> > > >
> > > > likelihood contributions to the overall likelihood in what might be considered an “integrated model”
> > > >
> > > > (Chapter 10). Modeling Type 3 data is discussed in Section 7.4 below."

Dear Marc,

Thank you so much for the clarification. By boundary estimates, I am assuming the probability values (please correct me if I am wrong). The false-positive probability values for both the males and females when calculated through both R and PRESENCE results showed similar values of probability (0.00 for males and 0.0103 for females). Though the standard errors were high in both cases for beta estimates.

Thank you
Prashant

On Tuesday, June 21, 2022 at 12:24:18 PM UTC+5:30 Kery Marc wrote:
>
> Dear Prashant,
>
>
>
> thanks, this is interesting. Now, the gender effect are wonky in both analyses. They may correspond to so-called boundary estimates, i.e., when the estimate of a proportion falls exactly on 0 and 1. Then, the maximum likelihood estimates are not to be trusted. Such problems can be “weakly” diagnosed by parameter estimates that are large in absolute terms (e.g., about > 5 or so) and more still by SE estimates that are large (e.g., 10 or higher).
>
>
>
> So, you ought to check whether the gender effect is estimable or whether perhaps all males have only nondetections and all females only detections.
>
>
>
> Best regards  -- Marc

> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > "Data can be of three types and are
> > > > >
> > > > > specified using the “type” argument in unmarkedFrameOccuFP. Occasions are defined to belong to
> > > > >
> > > > > one of the three data types and all or multiple data types can be combined into the same model.
> > > > >
> > > > > For Type 1 data, the detection process is assumed to meet the assumptions of the standard occupancy
> > > > >
> > > > > model where only false-negative errors occur, and false-positive detections are assumed to be absent. If all
> > > > >
> > > > > your data are of this type only, you should use the occu function. The detection parameter p, which is
> > > > >
> > > > > modeled using the detformula, is the only observation model parameter for these data.
> > > > >
> > > > > For Type 2 data, both false-negative and false-positive detection errors are allowed. If all data are
> > > > >
> > > > > of this type, the likelihood follows Royle and Link (2006). Both p (the true-positive detection
> > > > >
> > > > > probability, called p11 in our notation here) and the false-positive detection probability, p10 in our
> > > > >
> > > > > notation, described by fpformula, are estimated. In unmarked, the parameter p10 is labeled fp.
> > > > >
> > > > > For Type 3 data, observations include both certain detections (known to be true positives) and
> > > > >
> > > > > uncertain detections (that may be false positives). For the former we use the terms “certified,”
> > > > >
> > > > > “verified,” or “confirmed” detections synonymously to indicate that a detection is known to be a true
> > > > >
> > > > > positive. The observation model for Type 3 data contains the parameters p11 and p10 but, in addition,
> > > > >
> > > > > contains the new parameter b which is the probability that a true positive detection is verified to be
> > > > >
> > > > > certain. Miller et al. (2011) termed the model for Type 3 data to be a “multiple detection state”
> > > > >
> > > > > modeldbecause detections are represented by two distinct states, certain and uncertain, leading to a
> > > > >
> > > > > multi-state model. In contrast, when both Type 1 and Type 2 data occur together, the estimator is
> > > > >
> > > > > equivalent to the "multiple detection method" model described in Miller et al. (2011), which is just a
> > > > >
> > > > > traditional two-state occupancy model, but where p10 is assumed to be 0 for part of the data. Of course,
> > > > >
> > > > > all three types of data can be accommodated together in the same model, and this would be a “multiple
> > > > >
> > > > > detection-state, multiple method” model. On the other hand, each of the types could be thought of as
> > > > >
> > > > > simply a different method, producing independent data sets which are included together as distinct
> > > > >
> > > > > likelihood contributions to the overall likelihood in what might be considered an “integrated model”
> > > > >
> > > > > (Chapter 10). Modeling Type 3 data is discussed in Section 7.4 below."
> > > > >
> > > > >

> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > "We declare the two different data types via the type argument. The data are organized such that
> > > > >
> > > > > occasions 1-3 represent the Type 1 data from method 1, and occasions 4-7 are the Type 2 data from
> > > > >
> > > > > method 2.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > type <- c(nsurveys1, nsurveys2, 0)
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > When creating the unmarkedFrameOccuFP data object note that Method must be defined as an
> > > > >
> > > > > observational covariate. Note also that we could model variation in p10 using site or observation
> > > > >
> > > > > covariates.
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > summary(umf1 <- unmarkedFrameOccuFP(y = y, obsCovs = list(Method = Method),
> > > > >
> > > > > type = type)) # not shown"

> > > > >

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I want to get my head into prior regularization for the Bayesian occupancy models, I have read several papers on it including Hooten & Hobbs, 2015 <https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1890/14-0661.1>; Hutchinson et al., 2015 <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.12368> and Northrup & Gerber 2018 <https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0192819#pone.0192819.s007>. I kind of understood the idea, however, I am still struggling a little bit to implement it in my code. I also did not encounter any code examples so far. If anyone has an example code on prior regularization (preferably occupancy modeling but any would do) and would like to share it I'd be really grateful.

Thank you in advance.
Best,
Dilsad

--
A. Dilsad Dagtekin
PhD Student at Population Ecology Research Group
University of Zurich, Department of Evolutionary Biology and Environmental Studies
dilsad....@ieu.uzh.ch | www.popecol.org <http://www.popecol.org>
Ecology and Evol. Biology Society of Turkey: www.ekoevo.org <http://www.ekoevo.org>
ITU Alumni '16 & '18 | AFS Alumni '12

messages.subject: Error: Unequal number of secondary periods in each primary period
messages.subject_clean: Error: Unequal number of secondary periods in each primary period
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone!

I have data from 4 years of camera trap surveys. Almost every year has been surveyed twice, one on spring-summer and the other on fall-winter; except for one year has two surveys on fall-winter and one on summer. My objetive is to know which  environment my target species uses and if its influenced by antropogenic disturbance and distance to water.
With camtrapR I've filtered the events for 24hs and that's my record table called "g".
I've done the camera operation matrix and the detection history as follows:

Cam_Op<-cameraOperation(CTtable = CT,
                        stationCol = "Station",
                        sessionCol = "Session",
                        setupCol = "Setup_date",
                        retrievalCol = "Retrieval_date",
                        hasProblems = TRUE,
                        camerasIndependent = TRUE,
                        dateFormat = "dmy HM",
                        writecsv = TRUE,
                        outDir = "C:/Users/romina")

Det_Hist <- detectionHistory(recordTable = g,
                             camOp = Cam_Op,
                             output = "binary",
                             stationCol = "Station",
                             speciesCol = "Species",
                             species = "gato",
                             recordDateTimeCol = "DateTimeOriginal",
                             recordDateTimeFormat = "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S",
                             occasionLength = 1,
                             day1 = "station",
                             includeEffort = TRUE,
                             scaleEffort = FALSE,
                             datesAsOccasionNames = FALSE,
                             unmarkedMultFrameInput = TRUE,
                             timeZone = "America/Buenos_Aires",
                             writecsv = TRUE,
                             outDir = "C:/Users/romina")

Then, when I want to start with the modeling. I call the detection history since the format that gives the previous code is not read by the function unmarkedMultFrame

Det_Hist2<-read.csv("gato__detection_history__with_effort__1_days_per_occasion__occasionStart0h__first_day_by_station__2022-06-24.csv")

I charge the covariates of the sites wich are distances to water, sites with antropogenic disturbance and plant cover:

sitecovs<-read.csv2("Covariables fijas.csv")

And finally I tried to make the multiframe with the covariates included
umf <- unmarkedMultFrame(y=Det_Hist2, siteCovs=sitecovs, obsCovs=NULL, numPrimary=4, yearlySiteCovs=NULL)

but then this error apears: "Unequal number of secondary periods in each primary period"

I understand that my primary periods are the years (4) and secondary periods are the surveys made within those years. Then my question is, should I unify those two sampling periods of fall-winter? They are one in april and the other in July, then I should say that my cameras malfuntioned the time between those two surveys (which is not true) Or maybe I did something wrong in the code before the last step?

Thank you in advance,
Best, Romina

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jim, thank for your reply.

When I say that I filtered the events by 24 hs what I mean is that the record table took independent events those separate for 24hs.  I think my problem was that I mistook in the definition of my secondary sampling period. I used as reference examples of single season occupancy models, then I used 1 day as occasion and for my data I should use a period larger than that. How long? I don't know yet, but I'm working on that ;)

Best, Romina
